text:
Supermarkets compete hard for shoppers, and researchers have been studying what makes people buy more. In one study, shoppers spent longer in the store and bought more when slow music was playing. When the store smelled of freshly baked bread, sales of bakery items rose. Brighter lighting over the fruit made it seem fresher to shoppers.
Which one of the following is a conclusion that can be drawn from the above passage?
options: Supermarkets may be able to increase sales by changing the atmosphere of the store.
Shoppers choose a supermarket only on price.
Supermarkets should stop baking bread in the store.
Shoppers are aware of the music being played.
The atmosphere of a store matters more than the quality of its products.
solution: Each finding shows a change in the store's surroundings (music, smell, light) changing what people bought or felt, so altering the atmosphere may raise sales. The passage says nothing about price, gives no reason to stop baking, does not say shoppers noticed the music, and never compares atmosphere with product quality.

text:
Five children each eat one yoghurt every day for 14 days: two always eat strawberry and three always eat vanilla. Exactly the number of yoghurts needed is bought at the start. Packs contain one flavour only.

| pack | price |
|---|---|
| single yoghurt | €0.40 |
| pack of 4 | €1.40 |
| pack of 8 | €2.60 |
| pack of 12 | €3.60 |
| pack of 20 | €5.80 |

What is the most that can be saved by buying the best combination of packs and singles, compared with buying only single yoghurts?
solution: Needed: 28 strawberry and 42 vanilla, 70 in all, which as singles cost €28.00. Larger packs are cheaper per yoghurt. Strawberry 28 = 20 + 8: €5.80 + €2.60 = €8.40. Vanilla 42 is not a multiple of 4, so 2 must be singles; the cheapest 40 is 20 + 20 = €11.60, plus €0.80: €12.40. Total €20.80, a saving of €7.20. (€20.80 is the cost, not the saving.)

text:
The cheetah is the fastest land animal, reaching over 100 km/h, but it can keep up that speed for less than a minute. A horse is much slower at full speed, yet it can travel at a steady pace for hours. So why should top speed be the test of a good runner? The Arctic tern, which is not especially fast, flies tens of thousands of kilometres every year on migration.
Which one of the following is a conclusion supported by the above passage?
options: Cheetahs are the best runners among land animals.
Horses could run faster if they were trained.
Being fast over a short distance and travelling a long way are different abilities.
Birds are better travellers than mammals.
Speed is of no use to animals.
solution: The examples all separate speed from distance: the fastest animal tires quickly, while slower animals cover far more ground. That supports the idea that the two are different abilities. The passage questions using speed as the only test, so it does not crown the cheetah, says nothing about training, makes no general claim about birds and mammals, and does not say speed is useless.

text:
Action must be taken now to protect bees. Experts agree that banning a group of pesticides would help bee populations to recover. Safer pesticides are being developed, but they will not be available for at least eight years. The only way to protect bees now is to ban these pesticides.
Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the above argument?
options: Some farmers say their crop yields would fall if the pesticides were banned.
Bees are also harmed by disease and by the loss of wild flowers.
The pesticides are cheaper than the alternatives.
In a trial, bee colonies near fields where the pesticides were withdrawn grew by a third within two years.
Other pollinating insects are not affected by the pesticides.
solution: The argument depends on a ban actually helping bees. A trial in which bee colonies grew after the pesticides were withdrawn is direct evidence for that. Farmers' concerns and the low price of the pesticides are reasons against a ban; other threats to bees suggest a ban may not be the only answer; and other insects being unaffected is irrelevant.

text:
Anna cycles to work along a straight road at a steady speed, passing first the library and then a café. The whole ride normally takes her 48 minutes. Today she stopped for 5 minutes at the library and 4 minutes at the café.
Cycling at her usual speed, it takes 36 minutes to ride from her home to the café, and 28 minutes from the library to her work.
How long does the ride from the library to the café take?
solution: The stops do not change riding times, so ignore them. Home to work is 48 minutes and home to the café 36, so the café to work is 12 minutes. The library to work is 28 minutes, so the library to the café is 28 - 12 = 16 minutes. (Home to the library is 48 - 28 = 20 minutes, and 20 + 16 + 12 = 48 checks.)

text:
The table shows which types of paint are suitable for different surfaces.

| surface | water-based | oil-based | spray | epoxy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| wood | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| metal | no | yes | yes | yes |
| plastic | no | no | yes | yes |
| glass | no | no | no | yes |
| concrete | yes | yes | no | yes |

Which one of the following statements is supported by the table?
options: Epoxy is the only type of paint listed that can be used on glass.
Water-based paint can be used on metal.
Spray paint can be used on every surface listed.
Plastic can be painted with three of the four types of paint.
Oil-based paint is suitable for exactly two of the surfaces.
solution: The glass row has a "yes" only under epoxy. Water-based paint is "no" for metal; spray paint is "no" for glass and concrete; plastic takes only two types (spray and epoxy); and oil-based paint suits three surfaces (wood, metal and concrete).

text:
A carpet fitter charges a fixed amount per square metre of carpet laid and a fixed amount per metre of edging strip fitted around the edge of the room. For a rectangular room 4 m by 3 m, he charges €96 for the carpet and €28 for the edging.
At the same rates, what is his total charge for a rectangular room 6 m by 5 m?
solution: First room: 12 m² of carpet for €96 is €8 per m², and a perimeter of 14 m for €28 is €2 per metre. Second room: 30 m² x €8 = €240, and a perimeter of 22 m x €2 = €44. Total €284. Scaling the whole €124 bill by the area alone (x 2.5 = €310) ignores that the edging grows with the perimeter, not the area.

text:
A large dam built on a river flooded several villages and destroyed farmland that many poor families depended on. Despite this, governments still do not take the risks of large dams seriously. Until we can be sure that new dams will be planned to protect the people who live nearby, no new large dams should be built.
Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the above argument?
options: The risks of large dams were known before this dam was built.
The company that built the dam paid compensation to the families who lost their homes.
Without new dams, the region would burn more coal, causing greater harm to the same poor communities.
Future dams are likely to be planned more carefully than this one.
Solar power may one day replace hydroelectric power.
solution: The argument wants to stop new dams to protect poor communities. If stopping them would harm those same communities more, through pollution from coal, the ban defeats its own purpose. Known risks support the argument's complaint; compensation for one dam does not answer the general claim; better future planning is only a hope; and solar power may come one day but does not help now.

text:
A 300 g box holds identical cereal bars. The label says that 100 g provides 480 kcal and that one bar provides 72 kcal.
How many bars are in the box?
solution: One bar gives 72/480 = 0.15 of the energy in 100 g, so it weighs 15 g. A 300 g box holds 300/15 = 20 bars. 15 is the mass of one bar, not the number of bars.

text:
Two cyclists are 60 km apart and ride straight towards each other, one at 12 km/h and the other at 18 km/h. At the start, a dog runs from the first cyclist to the second at 25 km/h, turns straight back to the first, and keeps running back and forth until the cyclists meet.
How far does the dog run altogether?
solution: There is no need to add up the trips. The cyclists close the gap at 12 + 18 = 30 km/h, so they meet after 60/30 = 2 hours. The dog runs for those 2 hours at 25 km/h: 50 km.

text: The Elements, a treatise on geometry used as a textbook for more than two thousand years, was written by
solution: Euclid of Alexandria wrote the Elements around 300 BC, building geometry step by step from definitions and axioms. Archimedes worked on areas, volumes and buoyancy; Galileo and Newton came almost two thousand years later; Pythagoras left no writings of his own.

text: Which pair of country and name of its parliament (or lower house) is NOT correct?
solution: The Knesset is Israel's parliament; Spain's is the Cortes Generales (the Congress of Deputies and the Senate). The other pairs are correct; Iceland's Althing, founded in 930, is often called the oldest parliament in the world.

text:
A healthy person stands outside on a freezing day. Which of the following can happen in their body as a result?
1 Skeletal muscles start shivering.
2 Arterioles supplying the skin widen.
3 The metabolic rate rises.
solution: In the cold the body makes and keeps heat. Shivering releases heat from muscle respiration (1), and hormones such as thyroxine and adrenaline raise the metabolic rate (3). The skin arterioles NARROW (vasoconstriction) to keep warm blood away from the surface; widening is the response to heat. So 1 and 3 only.

text:
Adult haemoglobin is made of four polypeptide chains, two alpha and two beta, each folded around a haem group.
Which describes ONE beta chain on its own?
options: It has only a sequence of amino acids, with no folding.
It has helices but no overall 3-D fold.
It has an overall 3-D fold, but no quaternary structure.
It has no secondary structure, because the haem group replaces it.
solution: A single chain has a sequence of amino acids (primary), local helices (secondary) and an overall 3-D fold (tertiary). Quaternary structure is the arrangement of SEVERAL chains together, so it exists only in the assembled four-chain molecule, not in one chain.

text:
Which of the following produce genetic variation among the sperm cells made by one man?
1 crossing over between homologous chromosomes in prophase I
2 independent assortment of chromosome pairs in meiosis I
3 mitosis of the cells in the testes that later enter meiosis
solution: Crossing over swaps sections between maternal and paternal chromatids, and independent assortment shuffles which member of each pair goes into which cell. Both happen in meiosis and make every sperm different. Mitosis copies cells exactly, so it adds no variation (barring mutation). So 1 and 2 only.

text:
In a dividing cell from a diploid animal, the chromosomes are lined up one by one along the equator. Each is made of two chromatids, and the cell holds only half the species' usual number of chromosomes.
Which stage is this?
solution: Half the chromosome number means the cell has already been through meiosis I. Chromosomes still made of two chromatids and lined up singly on the equator is metaphase II. In metaphase I they line up as homologous PAIRS, and in mitosis the cell keeps the full number.

text:
Genes J, K, L and M lie on the same chromosome. The crossover values between pairs of them are:
J and K: 8%
K and L: 12%
J and L: 20%
L and M: 5%
K and M: 17%
Which order of the genes along the chromosome fits these values?
solution: Crossover values add along the chromosome. J-K (8) + K-L (12) = J-L (20), so K lies between J and L. K-L (12) + L-M (5) = K-M (17), so L lies between K and M. The order is J, K, L, M. In KJLM, K to L would be 28%, not 12%.

text: Which statement is correct while the atria of a healthy heart are contracting (atrial systole)?
options: The impulse is spreading through the Purkyne fibres.
solution: Atrial systole tops up the ventricles, so blood must pass through open atrioventricular valves, and the ventricles end it nearly full. The ventricles are still relaxed with their semilunar valves shut. The impulse reaches the Purkyne fibres only after the delay at the atrioventricular node, when the ventricles are about to contract.

text:
Penicillin is shaped like the substrate of a bacterial enzyme that cross-links the peptidoglycan of the cell wall. It binds to the enzyme's active site and does not let go.
Which of the following statements may be correct?
1 Penicillin inhibits this enzyme.
2 Bacteria treated while they are growing make weak walls and may burst by osmosis.
3 Penicillin also damages the cell walls of human cells.
solution: Binding the active site blocks the enzyme, so penicillin is an inhibitor (1). Without cross-links, a growing bacterium's wall is weak and water entering by osmosis can burst the cell (2). Human cells have no cell wall and no peptidoglycan, so 3 is wrong; that is why penicillin is safe to take. 1 and 2 only.

text:
A section of double-stranded DNA contains 200 nucleotides, and 30% of the nucleotides contain guanine.
How many hydrogen bonds hold the two strands together, and how many phosphodiester bonds does the section contain?
solution: G = 30% of 200 = 60 and C = 60, leaving 80 for A and T, so 40 each. That makes 60 G-C pairs (3 hydrogen bonds each, 180) and 40 A-T pairs (2 each, 80): 260 in all. Each strand is 100 nucleotides joined by 99 phosphodiester bonds, so the two strands have 198.

text:
Haemophilia A is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. A girl, Y, has haemophilia. Assume no new mutations.
Which of the following statements must be correct?
1 Her father has haemophilia.
2 Her mother has haemophilia.
3 If she has sons, they will all have haemophilia.
4 Her mother carries at least one copy of the allele.
solution: An affected girl is \(X^hX^h\): one \(X^h\) from each parent. Her father's only X carries it, so he is affected (1). Her mother has at least one copy (4) but could be a carrier, so 2 need not be true. Each son gets one of her X chromosomes, both \(X^h\), so every son is affected (3). So 1, 3 and 4.

text: Which one of these structures contains no smooth muscle, no ciliated epithelium and no cartilage?
options: the wall of the small intestine
solution: An alveolus is a thin sac of squamous (flattened) epithelium with elastic fibres and surrounding capillaries: no cartilage, no cilia, no smooth muscle. The trachea and bronchi have all three; the oviduct has ciliated epithelium and smooth muscle; the gut wall has smooth muscle layers.

text:
A girl with an inherited immune disorder (SCID) is treated by inserting a working copy of the faulty gene into some of her white blood cells. The treatment works, but her future children could still inherit the disorder.
Which of the following explain(s) this?
1 The working gene was not put into her eggs or into the cells that make them.
2 The working allele is recessive.
3 Genes inserted into white blood cells are copied by mitosis into every cell of the body, including eggs.
solution: This is somatic gene therapy: only the treated white blood cells and their descendants carry the new gene, and her eggs keep the faulty allele (1). The working allele is the dominant one, which is why one copy treats the disorder (2 wrong). Mitosis in white blood cells cannot put a gene into eggs (3 wrong). 1 only.

text:
Which of the following release a secretion containing an enzyme that digests starch?
1 salivary glands
2 pancreas
3 liver
solution: Saliva contains salivary amylase and pancreatic juice contains pancreatic amylase; both break starch into maltose. The liver makes bile, which has no digestive enzymes: its salts emulsify fats. So 1 and 2 only.

text:
An organism has these features:
Its cells have walls containing chitin.
It has no chloroplasts.
It releases enzymes onto its food and absorbs the products.
It reproduces by spores.
Which one of the following statements about the organism is correct?
options: It is a prokaryote that photosynthesises.
It is a plant that has lost its chlorophyll.
It is a eukaryote that feeds by digesting its food outside its cells.
It is an animal that takes food into a gut.
solution: Chitin walls, spores and external digestion followed by absorption are the marks of a fungus, a eukaryote. With no chloroplasts it cannot photosynthesise; plant walls are cellulose; animals have no cell walls and digest inside a gut; a virus has no cells at all.

text:
Which of the following contain glycosidic bonds?
1 glycogen in liver cells
2 cellulose in a plant cell wall
3 triglycerides in fat tissue
4 sucrose in sugar cane
solution: Glycosidic bonds join sugar units. Glycogen and cellulose are polysaccharides of glucose, and sucrose is glucose joined to fructose. Triglycerides are glycerol joined to three fatty acids by ESTER bonds, with no sugar. So 1, 2 and 4.

text:
During a bacterial infection, what would macrophages typically do?
1 engulf bacteria by phagocytosis
2 display antigens from digested bacteria on their cell surface
3 secrete antibodies against the bacteria
solution: Macrophages are phagocytes: they engulf and digest bacteria, then present pieces (antigens) on their surface to activate lymphocytes. Antibodies are secreted by plasma cells, which come from B lymphocytes. So 1 and 2 only.

text:
A grass, P, and a broad-leaved weed, Q, grow together in a field and compete for light and water. The field is sprayed with a herbicide that kills only broad-leaved plants.
Which of the following could happen as a result?
1 The population of P increases.
2 Competition for light between P and Q decreases.
3 P stops photosynthesising.
solution: With most of Q killed, P has more light, water and space, so its population can grow (1), and with fewer Q plants there is less competition between them (2). The herbicide does not affect grasses, so P keeps photosynthesising (3 wrong). 1 and 2 only.

text:
The template strand of a short gene reads, from 3' to 5':
TAC CTA GGT
What are the anticodons of the three tRNA molecules that bring the amino acids, in order?
solution: The mRNA is complementary to the template: 5'-AUG GAU CCA-3'. Each anticodon is complementary to its codon, which brings you back to the template's sequence, with U in place of T: UAC, CUA, GGU. AUG GAU CCA are the codons, and anything with T is DNA, not tRNA.

text:
Which of the following statements about a mature red blood cell in a healthy human is/are correct?
1 It contains haemoglobin.
2 It has a copy of the insulin gene.
3 It makes most of its ATP by aerobic respiration.
solution: A mature red blood cell is packed with haemoglobin but has lost its nucleus, so it carries no genes at all (2 wrong), and it has no mitochondria, so it relies on glycolysis, which is anaerobic (3 wrong). Most other body cells do carry the insulin gene, even though only beta cells use it. 1 only.

text:
Here are four compounds of nitrogen:
\(\mathrm{NH_3 \quad N_2O \quad NO_2 \quad HNO_3}\)
Which list gives exactly the oxidation states of nitrogen found in these compounds?
solution: With H = +1 and O = -2: in \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) N is -3; in \(\mathrm{N_2O}\) two N share +2, so +1 each; in \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) N is +4; in \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\), +1 + N - 6 = 0 gives +5. So -3, +1, +4 and +5. (+2 belongs to NO, which is not in the list.)

text: At 298 K and 1 atm, which of the following substances dissolves best in the liquid given?
solution: Like dissolves like. Ammonia is polar and hydrogen-bonds with water, so it is extremely soluble (hundreds of litres of gas per litre of water). Iodine and paraffin wax are non-polar and barely dissolve in water, oxygen dissolves only slightly, and an ionic solid like sodium chloride does not dissolve in non-polar hexane.

text:
Which pair of particles have the same number and arrangement of electrons in their ground states?
[Atomic numbers: F = 9; Na = 11; Mg = 12; Al = 13; S = 16; Cl = 17; Ar = 18; K = 19; Ca = 20]
solution: Count electrons. \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\): 20 - 2 = 18; \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\): 17 + 1 = 18, both with the argon arrangement. The others are mixed 10s and 18s: \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) 10 vs \(\mathrm{S^{2-}}\) 18, \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) 10 vs \(\mathrm{K^+}\) 18, \(\mathrm{F^-}\) 10 vs \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) 18, \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\) 10 vs Ar 18.

text:
Five atoms are shown. The letters are not chemical symbols.
Which atom has the highest first ionisation energy?
solution: Only the atomic number matters: these are C (6), N (7), O (8), Na (11) and Mg (12). Ionisation energy rises across period 2, but oxygen is the exception: its fourth p electron is paired, and repulsion makes it easier to remove, so nitrogen (about 1400 kJ/mol) beats oxygen (about 1310). Na and Mg, in period 3, are much lower.

text:
Which row correctly gives the geometry of the molecule and whether it has an overall dipole?

| | molecule | geometry | overall dipole |
|---|---|---|---|
| row 1 | \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) | linear | yes |
| row 2 | \(\mathrm{CCl_4}\) | tetrahedral | yes |
| row 3 | \(\mathrm{BF_3}\) | trigonal pyramidal | no |
| row 4 | \(\mathrm{CH_3Cl}\) | tetrahedral | yes |
| row 5 | \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) | bent | no |
solution: Chloromethane is tetrahedral, and the C-Cl bond differs from the three C-H bonds, so the dipoles do not cancel: polar. Water is bent, not linear; tetrachloromethane is symmetrical and non-polar; \(\mathrm{BF_3}\) is trigonal planar; \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) is linear. Row 4.

chapter: States of Matter and Gas Laws
text:
A sealed, rigid container holds an ideal gas at 27 °C.
To what temperature must it be heated for its pressure to become three times as large?
solution: At constant volume, pressure is proportional to ABSOLUTE temperature. 27 °C = 300 K, and tripling gives 900 K = 900 - 273 = 627 °C. Tripling the Celsius value (81 °C) is the trap, and 900 °C forgets to convert back.

text:
Ammonia reacts with water:
\(\mathrm{NH_3 + H_2O \rightleftharpoons NH_4^+ + OH^-}\)
Which statement about this reaction is correct?
options: Water acts as a Brønsted-Lowry base.
The solution formed has a pH below 7.
solution: Ammonia takes a proton from water, so ammonia is the base and water the acid. Adding that proton to \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) gives its conjugate acid, \(\mathrm{NH_4^+}\); water losing it gives its conjugate base, \(\mathrm{OH^-}\). The hydroxide ions make the solution alkaline, above pH 7.

chapter: States of Matter and Gas Laws
text:
A sealed, rigid container holds 2.0 mol of helium (treat it as an ideal gas).
What would raise the total kinetic energy of all the helium atoms in the container?
1 heating the gas from 300 K to 350 K
2 pumping in another 0.5 mol of helium at the same temperature
3 lifting the container onto a higher shelf
solution: The mean kinetic energy of the atoms is proportional to absolute temperature, so heating raises it (1). At the same temperature each atom keeps the same mean energy, but there are more atoms, so the total rises (2). Lifting the container gives it gravitational potential energy, not the atoms' random kinetic energy (3 wrong).

text:
Why does raising the temperature speed up a reaction between two gases?
1 The molecules collide more often.
2 A greater fraction of collisions have at least the activation energy.
3 The activation energy of the reaction becomes smaller.
solution: Faster molecules collide more often (1), and, more importantly, many more of them carry enough energy to react (2). The activation energy is fixed for a given pathway; only a catalyst lowers it, by providing a different route (3 wrong). 1 and 2 only.

text:
Which of the following statements about the Group VII elements (fluorine to iodine) is/are correct?
1 Chlorine can oxidise bromide ions to bromine.
2 The elements exist as diatomic molecules.
3 Their reactivity increases down the group.
solution: A halogen higher in the group displaces a lower one from its salts, so chlorine oxidises bromide to bromine (1). All the halogens form \(\mathrm{X_2}\) molecules (2). Reactivity DECREASES down the group, because the larger atoms attract an extra electron less strongly (3 wrong). 1 and 2 only.

subject: Mathematics
text:
The equation \(\dfrac{x+6}{x+2} = x\) has two roots.
What is their product?
solution: Multiply by \(x + 2\): \(x + 6 = x^2 + 2x\), so \(x^2 + x - 6 = 0\), which is \((x+3)(x-2) = 0\). The roots are -3 and 2, product -6 (as \(c/a\) also gives). Their sum, -1, is the other trap.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A pentagon is made of a rectangle 8 cm by 4 cm with an equilateral triangle of side 8 cm standing on one of its long sides.
What is the area of the pentagon?
solution: Rectangle: 8 x 4 = 32. An equilateral triangle of side \(a\) has area \(\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a^2 = \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \times 64 = 16\sqrt{3}\). Total \(32 + 16\sqrt{3} = 16(2 + \sqrt{3})\). Using \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 4\) for the triangle (giving 48) assumes its height is 4; it is \(4\sqrt{3}\).

subject: Physics
text:
A skydiver has been falling for some time and has reached terminal velocity.
Which describes the resultant force on the skydiver and their acceleration now?
solution: At terminal velocity air resistance has grown to equal the weight, so the forces balance and the resultant is zero. By Newton's second law, zero resultant force means zero acceleration: the speed stays constant. Gravity still acts, but it is cancelled.

subject: Mathematics
text: Find the line through the point (2, -1) that meets \(y = 3x - 5\) at right angles.
solution: Perpendicular gradients multiply to -1, so the new gradient is \(-\tfrac{1}{3}\). Through (2, -1): \(y + 1 = -\tfrac{1}{3}(x - 2)\), so \(3y + 3 = -x + 2\), giving \(x + 3y = -1\). \(3x - y = 7\) is parallel, \(x - 3y = 5\) has gradient \(+\tfrac{1}{3}\), and \(3x + y = 5\) has gradient -3; each of those passes through the point but at the wrong angle.

subject: Physics
text:
Three fibres have widths of 0.25 mm, 300 µm and \(2.8 \times 10^{-4}\) m.
Which order lists them from narrowest to widest?
solution: Convert all to micrometres: 0.25 mm = 250 µm, and \(2.8 \times 10^{-4}\) m = 0.28 mm = 280 µm. So 250, 280, 300: 0.25 mm, then \(2.8 \times 10^{-4}\) m, then 300 µm.

subject: Physics
text:
A uniform wire 3.0 m long has a circular cross-section of radius 0.50 mm. Its material has resistivity \(5.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \Omega\,\text{m}\).
What is the resistance of the wire?
solution: Area \(A = \pi r^2 = \pi (5.0 \times 10^{-4})^2 = 2.5 \times 10^{-7}\pi\ \text{m}^2\). \(R = \rho L/A = (5.0 \times 10^{-7} \times 3.0)/(2.5 \times 10^{-7}\pi) = 6/\pi\ \Omega\). Treating 0.50 mm as the diameter gives \(24/\pi\); forgetting to convert mm to m gives a wildly small answer.

subject: Physics
text:
Helium and argon are mixed in a container at 400 K. An argon atom has about ten times the mass of a helium atom.
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
1 Atoms of the two gases have the same mean kinetic energy.
2 Helium atoms have a greater mean square speed than argon atoms.
3 Argon atoms have the greater mean kinetic energy, because they are heavier.
solution: Mean kinetic energy depends only on temperature, so at the same temperature both gases have the same \(\tfrac{1}{2}m\langle v^2 \rangle\) (1, and 3 is wrong). With equal energy, the lighter helium atoms must have the larger \(\langle v^2 \rangle\), about ten times argon's (2). 1 and 2 only.

subject: Mathematics
text: Evaluate \((2 \times 10^{-2})^3 \times (5 \times 10^{6})\).
solution: Cube each part of the bracket: \(2^3 = 8\) and \((10^{-2})^3 = 10^{-6}\), so it is \(8 \times 10^{-6}\). Then \(8 \times 5 = 40\) and \(10^{-6} \times 10^{6} = 1\): the answer is 40, or \(4.0 \times 10^{1}\).
